reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the tumour suppressor gene TP53, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance
Characterised by a strikingly wide tumour spectrum, classically soft-tissue sarcoma, osteosarcoma, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma, and leukaemia
Cancers frequently develop in childhood and young adulthood, and affected individuals often develop multiple independent primary tumours over a lifetime
A family history clustering these core cancers across generations, especially with early onset, should prompt genetic evaluation and TP53 testing
Adrenocortical carcinoma or choroid plexus carcinoma in a child is a strong pointer to an underlying TP53 variant regardless of family history
Surveillance uses a whole-body and brain MRI-based protocol together with clinical review to detect tumours early, avoiding ionising radiation where possible
Therapeutic and diagnostic radiation should be minimised because irradiated tissue is prone to radiation-induced second malignancies
Risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy is offered for breast cancer risk, and management is coordinated through specialist cancer-genetics services
reference.pathophysiology: TP53 encodes the p53 protein, a central tumour suppressor that arrests the cell cycle, promotes DNA repair, and triggers apoptosis in response to genomic damage. A germline loss-of-function variant in one TP53 allele leaves cells vulnerable, and somatic loss or inactivation of the remaining allele removes this safeguard, allowing cells with damaged DNA to proliferate. The resulting genomic instability accounts for the early-onset, multi-site tumour predisposition, and the heightened sensitivity of p53-deficient tissue to DNA-damaging agents underlies the marked risk of radiation-induced second cancers.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (BRCA1/BRCA2)
Familial adenomatous polyposis with associated tumours
Sporadic early-onset cancer without a germline predisposition
Other hereditary sarcoma or brain tumour predisposition syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Germline TP53 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Whole-body MRI as part of a structured surveillance protocol
Dedicated brain MRI for central nervous system tumour surveillance
Breast MRI-based screening for at-risk women, favouring non-ionising imaging
Clinical examination, targeted symptom review, and biochemical assessment for adrenocortical tumours where indicated
redFlags: Childhood adrenocortical carcinoma or choroid plexus tumour suggesting an underlying TP53 variant
Multiple primary cancers in one individual, particularly the core LFS tumour types
New tumour arising within a previously irradiated field
Rapidly enlarging soft-tissue or bony mass in a young patient from an affected family
reference.prognosis: Prognosis reflects the lifetime risk of multiple malignancies, which is among the highest of the hereditary cancer syndromes, but intensive MRI-based surveillance improves early detection and survival. Outcomes for individual tumours depend on type and stage, and lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Attributing a young patient's cancer to chance and missing the underlying syndrome by not taking a detailed multigenerational family history
Using diagnostic or therapeutic ionising radiation liberally, thereby increasing second-cancer risk
Failing to offer surveillance and cascade testing to at-risk relatives
Overlooking a second primary tumour by assuming new symptoms represent recurrence of a known cancer
